title: LLD interview framework & rubric
relevance: High — the pacing + scoring model for every LLD / OOD / machine-coding round (campus + experienced); Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, PhonePe, Atlassian, Amazon, Google, Meta grade the same axes: problem analysis → class design → code quality → extensibility → communication.
company_notes: Campus/India product cos (Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, PhonePe, Cred, Ola) often put machine-coding first onsite at 90–120 min against the workat/Flipkart bar; FAANG/big-tech OOD–LLD (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft-style) lean discussion + class structure + extensibility on Hello Interview pacing, with formal UML uncommon and patterns only when justified; meta skill reused on every LLD problem (parking lot, Splitwise, elevator, games, booking).

phases.goal: Establish that LLD/OOD discussion and machine coding share one modeling skill, scored on a five-axis process rubric.

must_hit.point: Two formats, one skill: OOD/LLD discussion (45–60 min whiteboard/pseudocode) vs machine coding (60–120 min runnable demo)—same modeling, different design-heavy vs code-heavy time split.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both formats with those time ranges and says modeling is shared while pacing differs.

must_hit.point: Five rubric axes: Problem analysis (clarify, MUST vs NICE, out-of-scope); Class design (entities, ownership, APIs); Code quality (encapsulation, naming, SoC, composition over deep inheritance); Extensibility (absorb “add X” without rewrite / OCP); Communication (narrate tradeoffs, use-case trace).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all five axes with a one-line meaning for each.

must_hit.point: Announce the delivery pipeline: Requirements & scope → entities/relationships → class APIs (state + behavior) → core methods/demo → extensibility follow-ups; interviewers score process, not only the final diagram.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the pipeline in order and says process is graded alongside the diagram.

probes: What does an LLD interviewer actually grade, and how do OOD discussion rounds differ from machine coding?
Walk the delivery phases you would announce at the start of an LLD round.

hints.1: Start from two interview formats, then the scoring axes.
hints.2: Name the five Hello Interview axes, then the Requirements → Entities → APIs → demo → extensibility loop.
hints.3: Say: 45–60 min OOD vs 60–120 min machine coding, same modeling; score Problem analysis, Class design, Code quality, Extensibility, Communication; announce Requirements → entities → class APIs → demo → extensibility.

phases.goal: Lock requirements-first modeling: noun filter, state/behavior ownership, patterns-last, and the machine-coding demo bar.

must_hit.point: Requirements first: actors, ops, rules/state transitions, invalid inputs, concurrency if asked; write 4–8 bullets and never invent a notification engine nobody requested.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those requirement buckets, mentions a short bullet list, and refuses unsolicited features.

must_hit.point: Noun filter: nouns with state/rules become classes, mere info becomes field/enum, verbs become methods; aim ~4–7 core entities plus one orchestrator/Facade.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates classes from fields/enums and names an orchestrator alongside a small core entity set.

must_hit.point: Class design ties requirements → state → behavior; keep rules with the owner of the state (tell-don’t-ask); formal UML optional—ask; boxes + method stubs usually win.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Puts rules on the state owner and prefers boxes/stubs unless asked for formal UML.

must_hit.point: Patterns last and only when something varies (Strategy/Factory/Observer/State); 1–2 justified patterns beat five name-drops; over-engineering fails KISS/YAGNI.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Places patterns after APIs, limits to justified variation points, and cites KISS/YAGNI against pattern stuffing.

must_hit.point: Machine-coding bar: working + demonstrable, functionally correct, modular/readable, SoC, easy new requirements, Main/driver demo, graceful exceptions—UI/DB usually out of scope; mandatory > optional.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses Flipkart/workat language and says ship must-haves with a Main demo before optional polish.

probes: Given Design Parking Lot, how do you go from nouns to classes and where does the orchestrator sit?
When do you introduce a pattern, and what does a strong machine-coding demo need to show?

hints.2: Filter nouns into classes vs fields, bind rules to state owners, delay patterns until something varies.
hints.3: 4–8 requirement bullets → ~4–7 entities + Facade → state/behavior on owners → 1–2 patterns only if needed → working Main demo of must-haves.

phases.goal: Show judgment on time split, notation, patterns, and mandatory vs optional under the rubric.

must_hit.point: OOD discussion is design-heavy (class design often 10–15 min); machine coding is code-heavy (quick design ≤15–20% time, then bottom-up impl)—same entities/APIs, different depth of runnable code.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts the two time splits with those design budgets and says modeling stays the same.

must_hit.point: Communication > notation: offer boxes/stubs; switch to formal UML only if they insist—ceremony UML is not the default win.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers boxes/method stubs and upgrades to formal UML only on request.

must_hit.point: Mandatory > optional in machine coding: working must-haves beat half-finished extensibility; leave NICE as TODOs with comments and say what you’d add next.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prioritizes a clean demo of MUST features and parks NICE as commented TODOs.

probes: You have a Flipkart-style machine-coding round—how do you split design vs code time versus a Hello Interview OOD round?
Interviewer asks why you skipped full UML and whether you should finish optional features first.

hints.1: Compare the two formats’ clocks before defending notation or scope cuts.
hints.2: Boxes beat ceremony UML; ship MUST before NICE extensibility.
hints.3: OOD: 10–15 min class design; MC: ≤15–20% design then code; boxes/stubs unless asked; working must-haves + TODO NICE.

phases.goal: Run a timed attack script: requirements → entities → class design → implement/demo → verify and extensibility.

must_hit.point: Practice script: Requirements (3–5 min) MUST vs NICE sign-off → Entities (~3 min) noun-extract + orchestrator → Class design (10–15 min OOD / ≤15–20% MC) with 0–2 shared interfaces → implement 2–3 hot methods (OOD) or bottom-up enums→models→service→Main (MC).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites those phase time boxes and the OOD vs MC implementation difference.

must_hit.point: Close with verification & extensibility (last 5 min): one happy path + 2–3 edge cases (e.g. self-vote, full lot, illegal move); answer “add undo / new vehicle type / surge pricing” by pointing at the variation point, not rewriting.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Traces a scenario plus edge cases, then extends via an open interface/strategy.

must_hit.point: Timed dry run: 45 min OOD or 90 min machine coding on one awesome-LLD problem; score yourself aloud on the five rubric axes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks one format timer and self-scores Problem analysis through Communication.

probes: Design Tic-Tac-Toe—run only the first 3–5 minutes of requirements, then name your entities and orchestrator.
You have the last 5 minutes—verify a happy path and show how you’d add surge pricing without a rewrite.

hints.1: Treat it as a timed script with sign-off before coding.
hints.2: MUST/NICE → nouns/orchestrator → APIs/interfaces → hot methods or Main demo → trace + variation point.
hints.3: 3–5 min requirements → ~3 min entities → 10–15 min OOD design (or ≤15–20% MC) → 2–3 methods or bottom-up Main → last 5 min happy path + 2–3 edges + extensibility pointer; dry-run 45 or 90 min.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Same modeling skill; OOD (45–60 min) is design-heavy with pseudocode of 2–3 hot methods, machine coding (60–120 min) is code-heavy with ≤15–20% quick design then a runnable Main demo.
Default to boxes and stubs because communication beats notation; switch to formal UML only if the interviewer insists.
Introduce Strategy/Factory/Observer/State only after entities/APIs when something varies; 1–2 justified patterns beat five name-drops—over-engineering fails KISS/YAGNI on Code Quality.

tradeoffs.topic: Mandatory must-haves vs optional extensibility (machine coding)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ship working MUST features with a clean demo; leave NICE as TODOs with comments—half-finished extensibility loses to a demonstrable core.
Orchestrator/Facade coordinates; domain objects own rules (tell-don’t-ask)—neither dump-everything-in-Manager nor getters-only bags.

gotchas.trap: Skipping requirements and jumping straight to code.
gotchas.correction: Fails Problem Analysis; lock actors/ops/rules/MUST vs NICE and out-of-scope first.

gotchas.trap: Drawing full ceremony UML by default.
gotchas.correction: Communication > notation—offer boxes/stubs; use formal diamonds only if they insist.

gotchas.trap: Forcing Singleton/Factory everywhere before entities/APIs are clear.
gotchas.correction: Patterns come after class design, only at real variation points; unjustified patterns are a Code Quality red flag.
Orchestrator coordinates; domain objects own state rules—avoid dump-everything Manager and getters-only bags.

gotchas.trap: Finishing optional extensibility instead of a working demo in machine coding.
gotchas.correction: Mandatory > optional: working must-haves beat half-finished extensibility; say what you’d add next.

gotchas.trap: Answering “how would you extend this?” with “rewrite the whole thing.”
gotchas.correction: Point to the interface/strategy variation point you left open—rewrite fails Extensibility.
